Where it began

Harbhajan Singh was born in Jalandhar, in Punjab, on 3 July 1980, and grew up with five sisters. His first coach taught him to bat, and only later, under a new coach, did he turn to off-spin. It proved a sound change of plan.

He was 15 when he first played for the Punjab under-16 side, and in his first match against Haryana he took twelve wickets. Within months he was playing for India's under-19s. He made his first-class debut for Punjab in 1997 and his Test debut against Australia at Bangalore in 1998.

The player

The early years were stop and start, but in March 2001 everything changed. Australia arrived having won 16 Tests in a row. In Kolkata, Harbhajan dismissed Ricky Ponting, Adam Gilchrist and Shane Warne with consecutive balls, the first Test hat-trick by an Indian, and took 13 wickets in the match as India came back to win after following on. In Chennai he took 15 more, then walked out with India eight down and hit the winning runs. He finished that series with 32 wickets; none of his team-mates managed more than three.

Over a Test career from 1998 to 2015 he played 103 matches and took 417 wickets at 32.46, with 25 five-wicket innings and a best of 8 for 84.

What made him special

He bowled his off-spin with real skill, varying his pace and flight to tempt batsmen into mistakes. Give him a turning pitch in India and he could run through the best line-ups in the world. He was a lively, useful batsman too, fond of a six, and in Tests he made two hundreds with a highest score of 115.

Away from home the wickets sometimes came more slowly, and his Test batting average of 18.24 suggests the hundreds were treasured rather than routine. Each one was all the sweeter for it.

Away from the middle

He was in the India sides that won the World Twenty20 in 2007 and the World Cup in 2011, and that shared the Champions Trophy in 2002. In the IPL he spent ten years with Mumbai Indians, captaining them to the Champions League Twenty20 title in 2011, and later turned out for Chennai and Kolkata.

He received the Arjuna Award and the Padma Shri. Off the field he took to acting, television and the commentary box, and in 2023 he led Manipal Tigers to a Legends League title.

And finally

Twice in his early years he won a Test match award, and both times he finished the game with the bat, once with a straight six. For a man brought up as a batsman, it must have felt like the first coach had been right all along.
